tagline: Two arms of Grand Traverse Bay frame a ridge road.
intro: M-37 follows Center Road along the ridge of Old Mission Peninsula, with views of both arms of Grand Traverse Bay. Cherry orchards and vineyards occupy the peninsula between Traverse City and Old Mission Point. This northern section of M-37 is a Pure Michigan Scenic Byway. At its widest, the peninsula is about 3.25 miles across, with unusually steep terrain for this part of Michigan.

The route inland changed the way motorists traveled the peninsula. Beginning in the early 1940s, the Michigan State Highway Department built Center Road to improve access, replacing journeys along narrow, winding shoreline roads. Center Road became the northernmost leg of the state highway. A proposed transfer of the peninsula highway to local jurisdictions in 2019 raised the prospect of losing its byway status, which required a state trunkline road. MDOT canceled the transfer plans in 2021.

From Traverse City, the drive heads north along the peninsula’s middle. Mapleton lies roughly midway along M-37; farther north, Old Mission sits just east of the highway beside the East Arm of the bay. The northern end of the peninsula is flatter than the steep terrain farther south. The road finishes at a cul-de-sac in front of Mission Point Light, the 1870 lighthouse at the peninsula’s tip.

moments.title: Dougherty Mission House
moments.text: The Dougherty house began as a family home in 1842 and later became an inn. After Peter Dougherty moved his mission to Omena in 1852, the house remained unused until he sold it to Solon Rushmore in 1861. A later owner, Duranty Rushmore, turned it into the Rushmore House inn as tourism developed. The Rushmores added the front porch near the turn of the century. Peninsula Township bought the house in 2006 and began restoration; the log mission church nearby is a replica. Clapboard siding, cedar roof shingles and a fieldstone foundation distinguish the frame house from the nearby log church.

moments.title: Old Mission
moments.text: Old Mission takes its name from a mission that moved across the bay. In the 1836 Treaty of Washington, the federal government agreed to provide a mission and schools for local Ojibwe and Odawa communities. Indian agent Henry Schoolcraft selected a natural harbor on the peninsula’s eastern shore. Peter Dougherty established the mission in 1839, then relocated it to Omena in 1852. The community occupies Old Mission Harbor, a sheltered inlet of the East Arm of Grand Traverse Bay. Dougherty’s 1842 house and its surrounding structures now serve as a museum, preserving a physical link to the mission settlement.

moments.title: Mission Point Light
moments.text: Mission Point Light’s square tower is attached to a white wooden dwelling with black trim. Built in 1870, it copied the Mama Juda Light on the Detroit River, which has since been destroyed. Its job was to warn mariners of the shoals off the point. The lighthouse was decommissioned in 1933; a new offshore light was completed in 1938. The building stands a few hundred yards south of the 45th parallel, in the township-managed Lighthouse Park. Though only one and a half stories tall, its position on a sand bank raised the lens to 47 feet above the lake.
